The lighthouse at Raven’s Point is not a romantic place; it is a schedule. Every Monday, Elias Crowe (the keeper, now in his twenty-third year) wakes before the gulls, climbs the spiral stair with a lantern in one hand and a mug of tea in the other, and begins his rounds.

The routine never varies, and that is the point: a light must be kept, or the channel turns deadly. He checks the lens, the fuel, the glass — each in its turn — and marks the logbook with a small check that his father taught him to draw.

“People imagine I’m alone with my thoughts,” he told a visitor once. “The truth is we’re alone with the weather.” The weather is a demanding companion: fog for three days, then wind, then a stillness so complete you can hear the buoy bell a mile away.

Sunday is the day for small repairs: the dripping tap, the warped window frame, the hinge that moans in a gale. It isn’t heroism; it’s maintenance. The sea, Elias likes to say, respects maintenance more than courage, though the coast guard never agrees.

The supply boat arrives on Wednesday, weather permitting. Its crew calls out the mainland news: a wedding, a storm, a new teacher at the school. Elias listens, nods, and signs the receipt without looking up; the boat’s whistle is his only clock.

Once a month he reads the logbook aloud, from the first entry to the last. Why? Because a keeper who forgets his own history is no keeper at all. On those evenings he stays up late, and the lamp burns brighter than the law requires.

At midnight on Saturday he winds the clock, fills the lamp, and sets the wick with the old brass gauge. Then he stands at the rail and watches the beam sweep its patient circle. Don’t pity the keeper, the sexton wrote once; he keeps the light, and the light keeps him!
